<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:NBT}
Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois field extension with Galois group $G$. 
Then there exists an element $x \in L$ 
such that the family $(\sigma(x))_{\sigma\in G}$
forms a basis for $L$ as a vector space over $K$. In that case, 
$(\sigma(x))_{\sigma\in G}$ 
is called a 
normal basis for $L/K$, and
$x$ is called a 
normal basis generator for $L/K$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:CNBT}
Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois field extension with Galois group $G$. 
Then there exists an element
$x\in L$ which is a normal basis generator for $L/M$ for every intermediate 
field $K\subseteq M\subseteq L$.
In that case, the family 
$(\sigma(x))_{\sigma\in G}$ is called a completely normal basis for $L/K$, and
$x$ is called a 
completely normal basis generator
for $L/K$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:Lenstra}
Let $L/K$ be a Galois field extension with Galois group $G$. Then there
is a $G$-equivariant $K$-linear isomorphism
$C(G,K) \to L$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-field}
Let $L/K$ be a Galois field extension with Galois group $G$. Then there
exists a $G$-equivariant $K$-linear isomorphism
$\varphi:C(G,K) \to L$
such that, for every open subgroup $H$ 
of $G$, the induced
$H$-equivariant $L^H$-linear map
$\varphi^H:C(H,L^H) \to L$
is an isomorphism.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:affine-open}
Every surjective affine-linear map between finite-dimensional
affine $K$-spaces is open for the Zariski topology.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $q:A\to B$ be such a map and let $O\subseteq A$ be open.
For each $a\in O$, choose an affine-linear section $s:B\to A$
of $q$ satisfying $s(q(a))=a$.
Since $s$ is continuous, $s^{-1}(O)$ is an open neighborhood
of $q(a)$ contained in $q(O)$.
Thus $q(O)$ is open.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:small-open-intersection}
Let $K$ be an infinite field and let $A$ be a nonempty
finite-dimensional affine $K$-space.
If $\{O_\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda\}$ is a family of nonempty
Zariski-open subsets of $A$ with $|\Lambda|<|K|$, then
$\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda}O_\lambda\neq
\varnothing$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This follows by taking complements in
\cite[Theorem~3.14]{Ghosh2022} when $\dim A>0$.
If $\dim A=0$, then $A$ is a singleton and the assertion
is immediate.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:inverse-limit-divisibility}
Let $(X_n,T_{m,n})$ be an inverse system of nonempty finite
sets indexed by the positive integers ordered by divisibility.
Then $\varprojlim_n X_n\neq\varnothing$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The assertion is a special case of
\cite[Ch.~III, \S7, no.~4, Theorem~1]{BourbakiSets}.
For completeness, we give an elementary proof
adapted to the present setting.
For each $n\geq1$, put
$Y_n=\bigcap_{n\mid m}T_{m,n}(X_m)$.
Choose a multiple $d_n$ of $n$ with
$|T_{d_n,n}(X_{d_n})|$ minimal.
If $n\mid m$ and $r=\operatorname{lcm}(d_n,m)$, then
$
T_{r,n}(X_r)
\subseteq
T_{d_n,n}(X_{d_n})\cap T_{m,n}(X_m)$.
Minimality therefore gives
$T_{r,n}(X_r)=T_{d_n,n}(X_{d_n})$.
Thus,
$Y_n=T_{d_n,n}(X_{d_n})\neq\varnothing$,
and $T_{r,n}(X_r)=Y_n$ whenever $d_n\mid r$.
If $n\mid m$, choose a common multiple $r$ of $d_n$ and $d_m$.
Then $T_{m,n}(Y_m)
=T_{m,n}(T_{r,m}(X_r)) =T_{r,n}(X_r) =Y_n$.
Thus the restricted transition maps are surjective.
We may therefore choose recursively $y_k\in Y_{k!}$ such that
$T_{(k+1)!,k!}(y_{k+1})=y_k$ for every $k\geq1$.
Put $x_n=T_{n!,n}(y_n)$.
If $n\mid m$, the recursive relations give
$T_{m!,n!}(y_m)=y_n$, and hence
$T_{m,n}(x_m) =T_{m!,n}(y_m) =T_{n!,n}(y_n)=x_n$.
Consequently $(x_n)_{n\geq1}\in\varprojlim_n X_n$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:finite-liftable-extension}
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal, and let
$(X_i,p_{ji})_{i\in I}$ be an inverse system of
nonempty sets indexed by a directed set $I$
with $|I|\leq\kappa$.
Suppose that, whenever $S\subseteq I$ satisfies
$|S|<\kappa$ and $i\in I\setminus S$, every finitely
liftable family on $S$ extends to a finitely liftable
family on $S\cup\{i\}$.
Then, for every directed subset $J\subseteq I$
with $|J|<\kappa$, the restriction map
$\varprojlim_{i\in I}X_i \to \varprojlim_{j\in J}X_j$
is surjective.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix a directed subset $J\subseteq I$ with $|J|<\kappa$
and a coherent family $(a_j)_{j\in J}$.
This family is finitely liftable, since every finite
subset of $J$ has an upper bound in $J$.
We extend this family by transfinite recursion,
maintaining finite liftability by transfinite induction;
see \cite[Ch.~III, \S2, no.~2, C59--C60]{BourbakiSets}.

Write $I\setminus J=\{i_\alpha:\alpha<\mu\}$,
where $\mu=|I\setminus J|\leq\kappa$ is regarded
as its initial ordinal, and put
$S_\alpha=J\cup\{i_\beta:\beta<\alpha\}$
for $\alpha\leq\mu$.
To make the choices definite, fix a well-ordering
of $\bigcup_{i\in I}X_i$.
Start with $x_j=a_j$ for $j\in J$.
Suppose that $\alpha<\mu$ and a finitely liftable
family has been constructed on $S_\alpha$.
Since $|J|<\kappa$ and $|\alpha|<\mu\leq\kappa$,
we have $|S_\alpha|<\kappa$.
The hypothesis therefore allows us to choose
$x_{i_\alpha}\in X_{i_\alpha}$ so that the extended
family on $S_{\alpha+1}$ remains finitely liftable.
Choose the least such value in the fixed well-ordering.
At a nonzero limit stage $\lambda\leq\mu$, take
the union of the previously constructed families.
Every finite subset of $S_\lambda$ is contained
in some $S_\alpha$ with $\alpha<\lambda$.
Thus every finite subfamily already has a common
lift, and the union remains finitely liftable.
The recursion produces a finitely liftable family
$(x_i)_{i\in I}$ extending $(a_j)_{j\in J}$.
This family is coherent: if $i\leq j$, choose
a common lift $y\in X_k$ of $x_i$ and $x_j$.
Compatibility of the transition maps gives
$x_i = p_{ki}(y) = p_{ji}(p_{kj}(y))= p_{ji}(x_j)$.
                                                  
Hence $(x_i)_{i\in I}\in\varprojlim_{i\in I}X_i$
extends $(a_j)_{j\in J}$, proving surjectivity.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:cardinal-bounded-inverse-limit}
Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal, and let
$(X_i,p_{ji})_{i\in I}$ be an inverse system of
nonempty sets with surjective transition maps,
indexed by a directed set $I$ with $|I|\leq\kappa$.
For each $i\in I$, suppose that a collection
$\mathcal C_i$ of subsets of $X_i$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (i)]
$X_i\in\mathcal C_i$, and $\mathcal C_i$ is closed
under finite intersections.

\item[\rm (ii)]
Every subfamily of $\mathcal C_i$ of cardinality
less than $\kappa$ having the finite intersection
property has nonempty intersection.

\item[\rm (iii)]
For $i\leq j$ and $x\in X_i$, the fibre
$p_{ji}^{-1}(\{x\})$ belongs to $\mathcal C_j$.

\item[\rm (iv)]
For $i\leq j$ and $C\in\mathcal C_j$, the image
$p_{ji}(C)$ belongs to $\mathcal C_i$.
\end{enumerate}
Then, for every directed subset $J\subseteq I$ 
such that $|J|<\kappa$, the restriction map
$\varprojlim_{i\in I}X_i \to
\varprojlim_{j\in J}X_j$
is surjective.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-liftable-extension}, it
suffices to verify the extension property for
finitely liftable partial families.
Fix such a family $(x_j)_{j\in S}$ with
$|S|<\kappa$, and let $i\in I\setminus S$.

First observe that a finite family having a common
lift in some $X_\ell$ has a common lift in $X_k$
for every upper bound $k$ of its indices.
Indeed, choose $r\geq k,\ell$, lift the given
element from $X_\ell$ to $X_r$ using surjectivity,
and project to $X_k$.

For each finite $F\subseteq S$, choose an upper
bound $k$ of $F\cup\{i\}$. We now define
$C_F=
p_{ki}(
\bigcap_{j\in F}p_{kj}^{-1}(\{x_j\})).$
When $F=\varnothing$, the intersection inside
the parentheses is understood to be $X_k$.
Conditions~(i), (iii), and~(iv) imply that
$C_F\in\mathcal C_i$.

By the preceding observation, $C_F$ is independent
of the chosen upper bound $k$.
It consists precisely of those $u\in X_i$ such
that $u$ and $(x_j)_{j\in F}$ have a common lift.
Finite liftability and the same observation show
that $C_F\neq\varnothing$.
Moreover, for any finite subsets
$F_1,\ldots,F_r\subseteq S$, we have
$C_{F_1\cup\cdots\cup F_r}
\subseteq C_{F_1}\cap\cdots\cap C_{F_r}$.
Thus the family of all $C_F$ has the finite
intersection property.

Since $|S|<\kappa$, there are fewer than $\kappa$
finite subsets of $S$.
Condition~(ii) therefore allows us to choose
$x_i\in
\bigcap_{F\subseteq S, \ F\text{ finite}}C_F$.
In particular, $x_i\in C_{\varnothing}=X_i$.
For every finite $F\subseteq S$, membership in
$C_F$ means that $x_i$ and $(x_j)_{j\in F}$
have a common lift.
Hence adjoining $x_i$ preserves finite liftability.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:relative-affine-open-limit}
Let $K$ be an infinite field and let $(V_i,p_{ji})$ be an
inverse system of nonempty finite-dimensional affine
$K$-spaces with surjective affine-linear transition maps,
indexed by a directed set $I$ with $|I|\leq|K|$.
Let $U_i\subseteq V_i$ be nonempty Zariski-open subsets
satisfying $p_{ji}(U_j)=U_i$ whenever $i\leq j$.
Then, for every directed subset $J\subseteq I$ with
$|J|<|K|$, the restriction map
$\varprojlim_{i\in I}U_i \to \varprojlim_{j\in J}U_j$
is surjective.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Put $\kappa=|K|$. We apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:cardinal-bounded-inverse-limit}
to the inverse system $(U_i,p_{ji}|_{U_j})$.
For each $i\in I$, let $\mathcal C_i$ consist of
$\varnothing$ and all nonempty subsets of $U_i$
that are relatively Zariski open in some affine
subspace of $V_i$.

Clearly, $U_i\in\mathcal C_i$.
If finitely many members of $\mathcal C_i$ have
nonempty intersection, their intersection is relatively
Zariski open in the intersection of the corresponding
affine subspaces.
Since $\varnothing\in\mathcal C_i$, it follows that
$\mathcal C_i$ is closed under finite intersections.

For $i\leq j$ and $x\in U_i$, the fibre of
$p_{ji}|_{U_j}$ over $x$ is
$U_j\cap p_{ji}^{-1}(\{x\})$,
which is relatively Zariski open in the affine
subspace $p_{ji}^{-1}(\{x\})$ of $V_j$.
Hence this fibre belongs to $\mathcal C_j$.
Moreover, if $C\in\mathcal C_j$ is nonempty and
relatively Zariski open in an affine subspace
$B\subseteq V_j$, then
Lemma~\ref{lem:affine-open}, applied to
$p_{ji}|_B:B \to p_{ji}(B)$,
shows that $p_{ji}(C)$ is relatively Zariski open
in the affine subspace $p_{ji}(B)$.
Since $p_{ji}(C)\subseteq U_i$, we have
$p_{ji}(C)\in\mathcal C_i$.
The image of the empty set also belongs to
$\mathcal C_i$.

It remains to verify the intersection property.
Fix $i\in I$, and let
$\{C_\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda\}\subseteq\mathcal C_i$
have the finite intersection property, with
$|\Lambda|<\kappa$.
The case $\Lambda=\varnothing$ follows from
$U_i\neq\varnothing$, so assume $\Lambda\neq\varnothing$.
For each $\lambda$, choose an affine subspace
$A_\lambda\subseteq V_i$ in which $C_\lambda$
is relatively Zariski open.

For every nonempty finite $F\subseteq\Lambda$, put
$A_F=\bigcap_{\lambda\in F}A_\lambda$.
These affine subspaces are nonempty by the finite
intersection property.
Choose a nonempty finite $F_0\subseteq\Lambda$
for which $\dim A_{F_0}$ is minimal, and put
$A=A_{F_0}$.
For every $\lambda\in\Lambda$,  
$A_{F_0\cup\{\lambda\}} = A\cap A_\lambda\subseteq A$.
Minimality of dimension gives
$A\cap A_\lambda=A$, so $A\subseteq A_\lambda$.
Consequently, $C_\lambda\cap A$ is relatively
Zariski open in $A$.
It is also nonempty, since it contains
$\bigcap_{\nu\in F_0\cup\{\lambda\}}C_\nu$,
which is nonempty by the finite intersection property.

Lemma~\ref{lem:small-open-intersection} now gives
$\varnothing\neq
\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(C_\lambda\cap A)
\subseteq
\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda}C_\lambda$.
All hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:cardinal-bounded-inverse-limit}
are therefore satisfied, and the desired
surjectivity follows.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:relative-limit-counterexample}
The assumption $|J|<|K|$ in
Proposition~\ref{prop:relative-affine-open-limit}
cannot be replaced by $|J|\leq|K|$.
We adapt Waterhouse's example \cite{Waterhouse1972}.
Let $K$ be an infinite field, put $E=K\sqcup\{*\}$,
and let $I$ be the set of finite subsets of $E$,
ordered by inclusion.
Put $J=\{F\in I \mid F\subseteq K\}$.
Then $I$ and $J$ are directed and
$|I|=|J|=|K|$.
For $F\in I$, put $V_F=K^F$ and
$U_F=\{x\in K^F:x_a\neq x_b
       \text{ whenever }a,b\in F,\ a\neq b\}$.
These sets are nonempty and Zariski open.
The coordinate restriction maps are surjective linear
maps between the $V_F$ and are also surjective on
the $U_F$: every injection from a finite subset of
$E$ into $K$ extends to any larger finite subset,
since $K$ is infinite.
However, the coherent family
$(\operatorname{id}_K|_F)_{F\in J}$
cannot extend to an element of
$\varprojlim_{F\in I}U_F$.
Such an extension would define an injection $E\to K$
whose restriction to $K$ is the identity, leaving
no possible value for the additional element $*$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:units-open}
Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-algebra.
Then $A^\times$ is a nonempty basic Zariski-open
subset of the affine $K$-space $A$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $a\in A$, let $L_a:A\to A$ denote left
multiplication by $a$.
An element $a$ is invertible if and only if $L_a$
is invertible. Indeed, if $L_a$ is invertible, choose
$b\in A$ with $ab=1$; injectivity of $L_a$ then gives
$ba=1$.
The function $d:A\to K$, defined by
$d(a)=\det(L_a)$, is polynomial in linear coordinates.
Thus $A^\times=D(d)$, which is nonempty since $d(1)=1$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:unit-lifting-zariski}
Let $R$ and $S$ be finite-dimensional $K$-algebras,
and let $f:R\to S$ be a surjective $K$-algebra
homomorphism. Then $f(R^\times)=S^\times$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This holds more generally for surjective homomorphisms
from Artinian rings; see \cite[Lemma~(2.6)]{Lenstra}.
For completeness, we give a direct proof in two cases.
The inclusion $f(R^\times)\subseteq S^\times$ is immediate. Now we show the reverse inclusion.

Case 1: $K$ is infinite.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:units-open}, $R^\times$ is a
nonempty Zariski-open subset of $R$.
Since $f$ is surjective and $K$-linear,
Lemma~\ref{lem:affine-open} shows that
$H:=f(R^\times)$ is a nonempty Zariski-open subset
of $S$. Moreover, $H$ is a subgroup of $S^\times$.
Take $s\in S^\times$. Left multiplication by $s$
is a $K$-linear automorphism of $S$, so $sH$
is also nonempty and Zariski open in $S$.
Since $K$ is infinite, $H\cap sH\neq\varnothing$.
Thus $s=h_1h_2^{-1}\in H$ for some $h_1,h_2\in H$.
This proves $f(R^\times) \supseteq S^\times$.

Case 2: $K$ is finite.
Let $s\in S^\times$ and choose $a\in R$ with $f(a)=s$.
Since $R$ is finite-dimensional over the finite field
$K$, it is finite. The powers of $a$ are therefore
eventually periodic.
Taking $n$ sufficiently large and divisible by the
period gives $a^{2n}=a^n$.
Thus $e:=a^n$ is idempotent.
Since $f(e)=s^n$ is both a unit and an idempotent,
we have $f(e)=1$.
Put $u=ae+(1-e)$.
Since $a$ commutes with $e$, the two summands
annihilate one another, and
$u^n=(ae)^n+(1-e)=e+(1-e)=1$.
Hence $u\in R^\times$, and
$f(u)=f(a)f(e)+1-f(e)=s$.
This proves $f(R^\times) \supseteq S^\times$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:galois-finite-dimensional}
The $K$-algebra $S$ is finite-dimensional.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By \cite[Theorem~1.3(c)]{ChaseHarrisonRosenberg},
$S$ is finitely generated projective as an $R$-module.
Since $R$ is finite-dimensional over $K$, so is $S$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:normalbasissemilocal}
The extension $S/R$ has a $G$-normal basis.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $R$ is finite-dimensional over $K$, it is
Artinian and hence semilocal.
The assertion therefore follows from
\cite[Theorem~4.2(c)]{ChaseHarrisonRosenberg}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:Mazur-resolvent}
An element $x\in S$ is a $G$-normal basis
generator for $S/R$ if and only if
$\rho_G(x)\in S[G]^\times$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
This is a special case of
\cite[Proposition~1]{Mazur}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:normal-trace-lift}
Let $H\trianglelefteq G$. Then
$\operatorname{Tr}_H(\mathcal N_G(S/R)) = \mathcal N_{G/H}(S^H/R)$.
In particular,
$\operatorname{Tr}_G(\mathcal N_G(S/R))=R^\times$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $s\in\mathcal N_G(S/R)$ and put $t=\operatorname{Tr}_H(s)$.
Since $H$ permutes the $R$-basis
$(\sigma(s))_{\sigma\in G}$, the sums over its orbits
form an $R$-basis of $S^H$.
As $H$ is normal, these sums are precisely the
$G/H$-conjugates of $t$.
Thus $t\in\mathcal N_{G/H}(S^H/R)$, proving one
inclusion.
 
Conversely, let $x\in\mathcal N_{G/H}(S^H/R)$.
Choose $s\in\mathcal N_G(S/R)$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:normalbasissemilocal}, and put
$t=\operatorname{Tr}_H(s)$.
Since $x$ and $t$ are both normal basis generators,
there exist $v,w\in R[G/H]$ such that
$x=v(t)$ and $t=w(x)$.
Their normal basis properties give $wv=vw=1$,
so $v\in R[G/H]^\times$.
 
By Proposition~\ref{prop:unit-lifting-zariski},
the canonical surjection $R[G]\to R[G/H]$
lifts $v$ to some $u\in R[G]^\times$.
Put $y=u(s)$.
The map $R[G] \ni a \mapsto a(y)=(au)(s) \in S$
is an $R$-linear isomorphism, 
being the composite of right
multiplication by $u$ and the normal basis
isomorphism associated with $s$.
Hence $y\in\mathcal N_G(S/R)$.
Since $H$ is normal, the trace is compatible with
the quotient group-algebra action, so 
$\operatorname{Tr}_H(y)=v(\operatorname{Tr}_H(s))=v(t)=x$.
This proves the reverse inclusion.

Taking $H=G$ gives the final assertion, since
$\mathcal N_{\{e\}}(R/R)=R^\times$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:nonemptyzariskinb}
$\mathcal N_G(S/R)$ is a nonempty
Zariski-open subset of the affine $K$-space $S$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Nonemptiness follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:normalbasissemilocal}.
Since $S[G]$ is finite-dimensional over $K$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:units-open} shows that $S[G]^\times$
is Zariski open.
The map $\rho_G:S\to S[G]$ is $K$-linear and
hence Zariski continuous. Thus
Lemma~\ref{lem:Mazur-resolvent} gives
$\mathcal N_G(S/R)=\rho_G^{-1}(S[G]^\times)$,
which is Zariski open in $S$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:completenormalbasis}
Let $K$ be infinite.
Then $\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R)$ is a nonempty
Zariski-open subset of the affine $K$-space $S$.
In particular, $S/R$ has a $G$-completely normal basis.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For every subgroup $H\leq G$, the algebra $S^H$
is finite-dimensional over $K$, since it is a
$K$-subspace of $S$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:nonemptyzariskinb}, applied to the
$H$-Galois extension $S/S^H$, therefore shows that
$\mathcal{N}_H(S/S^H)$ is nonempty and Zariski open
in $S$.
Since $K$ is infinite, these subsets are dense.
As $G$ has only finitely many subgroups, their
intersection $\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R)$ is nonempty
and Zariski open.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:finite-field-no-complete-normal-basis}
The hypothesis that $K$ is infinite in
Theorem~\ref{thm:completenormalbasis} cannot be omitted.
Let $K=\mathbb F_3$, put $S=K\times K$, and let
$G=C_2=\{e,\tau\}$ act by $\tau(a,b)=(b,a)$.
Identifying $K$ with the diagonal subalgebra of $S$,
the extension $S/K$ is $G$-Galois.
If $x=(a,b)$ were a $G$-completely normal basis
generator, the condition for the trivial subgroup
would imply $x\in S^\times$, so $a,b\neq0$.
But then $\left|\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ b&a\end{smallmatrix}\right|
=a^2-b^2 = 1-1 = 0$,
so $(x,\tau(x))$ is not a $K$-basis of $S$.
Thus $\mathcal{CN}_G(S/K)=\varnothing$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace-preserves-complete-normality}
Let $H\trianglelefteq G$. Then
$\operatorname{Tr}_H(\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R))
\subseteq \mathcal{CN}_{G/H}(S^H/R)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $x\in\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R)$ and put $y=\operatorname{Tr}_H(x)$.
For every subgroup $V$ with $H\leq V\leq G$, we have
$x\in\mathcal{N}_V(S/S^V)$.
Since $H\trianglelefteq V$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-trace-lift}, applied to
$S/S^V$, gives $y\in\mathcal{N}_{V/H}(S^H/S^V)$.
Every subgroup of $G/H$ has the form $V/H$, and
$(S^H)^{V/H}=S^V$.
Thus $y\in\mathcal{CN}_{G/H}(S^H/R)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:complete-normal-trace-lift}
If $K$ is infinite and $H\trianglelefteq G$,
then $\operatorname{Tr}_H(\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R)) 
=\mathcal{CN}_{G/H}(S^H/R)$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-preserves-complete-normality},
it suffices to prove the reverse inclusion.
Fix $x\in\mathcal{CN}_{G/H}(S^H/R)$ and put
$\mathcal T_x=\{y\in S:\operatorname{Tr}_H(y)=x\}$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-trace-lift},
$\mathcal T_x$ is nonempty. Since $\operatorname{Tr}_H$ is
$K$-linear, $\mathcal T_x$ is a finite-dimensional
affine $K$-space.
For every subgroup $U\leq G$, put
$\mathcal O_U
=\mathcal T_x\cap\mathcal N_U(S/S^U)$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:nonemptyzariskinb},
$\mathcal O_U$ is Zariski open in $\mathcal T_x$.
We show that each $\mathcal O_U$ is nonempty.

Choose $s\in\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R)$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:completenormalbasis}.
Fix $U\leq G$, and put $I=U\cap H$ and $J=UH$.
Then $I\trianglelefteq U$, and the map
$uI\mapsto uH$ identifies $U/I$ with $J/H$.

Since $x$ is completely normal for $S^H/R$,
it is a $(J/H)$-normal basis generator for
$S^H/S^J$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Mazur-resolvent},
$\rho_{J/H}(x)$ is a unit of $S^H[J/H]$.
The inclusion $S^H\subseteq S^I$ and the preceding
group isomorphism induce a homomorphism
$S^H[J/H] \to S^I[U/I]$
carrying $\rho_{J/H}(x)$ to $\rho_{U/I}(x)$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Mazur-resolvent} again, we get
$x\in\mathcal N_{U/I}(S^I/S^U)$.
Since $s$ is completely normal,
Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-trace-lift} gives
$\operatorname{Tr}_U(s)\in(S^U)^\times$ and 
$\operatorname{Tr}_J(s)\in(S^J)^\times$. 

Consequently,
$c:=\operatorname{Tr}_J(s)^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_U(s)\in(S^U)^\times$,
and $cx$ is also a $(U/I)$-normal basis generator
for $S^I/S^U$.
Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:normal-trace-lift}
to $S/S^U$, we obtain
$y_U\in\mathcal N_U(S/S^U)$ with
$\operatorname{Tr}_I(y_U)=cx$.

Let $T\subseteq H$ be a set of representatives
for the left cosets of $I$ in $H$.
Since $J=HU$ and $I=H\cap U$, the same set
represents the left cosets of $U$ in $J$.
Both $x$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_J(s)$ are fixed by $H$, so
we get that
$
\operatorname{Tr}_H(y_U)
 =\sum_{\tau\in T}\tau(\operatorname{Tr}_I(y_U)) 
 =\sum_{\tau\in T}\tau(cx)
 =x\,\operatorname{Tr}_J(s)^{-1}
       \sum_{\tau\in T}\tau(\operatorname{Tr}_U(s))
 =x\,\operatorname{Tr}_J(s)^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_J(s)=x.
$
Therefore $y_U\in\mathcal O_U$, proving non\-emptiness.

Since $G$ has only finitely many subgroups and
$K$ is infinite, the nonempty open subsets
$\mathcal O_U$ of $\mathcal T_x$ have nonempty
intersection.
Any element of this intersection belongs to
$\mathcal{CN}_G(S/R)$ and has $H$-trace equal to $x$.
This proves the reverse inclusion.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:coherent-Lenstra-galois}
There is a natural bijection between trace-coherent
families $(x_N)_{N\in\mathcal U}$ satisfying
$x_N\in\mathcal{CN}_{G/N}(S^N/R)$, for 
$N\in\mathcal U$,
and $G$-equivariant $R$-linear isomorphisms
$\varphi:C(G,R)\to S$ such that $\varphi^H$ is an
isomorphism for every open subgroup $H\leq G$.
The correspondence is characterized by
$x_N=\varphi(1_N)$, where $1_N$ is the
characteristic function of $N$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
We first establish the correspondence for ordinary
normal basis generators.
Identify $(G/N,R)$ with $C(G,R)^N$ by inflation.
Given a trace-coherent family $(x_N)_{N\in\mathcal U}$
of normal basis generators, define
$\varphi_N : (G/N,R) \to  S^N$ by
$\varphi_N(f)
=\sum_{\sigma N\in G/N}f(\sigma N)\sigma(x_N)$.
Each $\varphi_N$ is a $(G/N)$-equivariant
$R$-linear isomorphism.
For $M\subseteq N$, grouping the terms in
$\varphi_M(f)$ according to the cosets of $N$
and using trace coherence gives
$\varphi_M(f)=\varphi_N(f)$ for
$f \in (G/N,R)$.
Since $C(G,R)$ and $S$ are the unions of these
finite-level function modules and fixed rings,
respectively, the maps $\varphi_N$ induce a
$G$-equivariant $R$-linear isomorphism
$\varphi:C(G,R)\to S$.

Conversely, let $\varphi:C(G,R)\to S$ be such an
isomorphism and put $x_N=\varphi(1_N)$.
Taking $N$-fixed points gives a $(G/N)$-equivariant
$R$-linear isomorphism
$(G/N,R) \to S^N$,
which sends the characteristic-function basis to
$(\sigma(x_N))_{\sigma N\in G/N}$.
Thus $x_N$ is a normal basis generator.
For $M\subseteq N$, the identity
$1_N=\sum_{\tau M\in N/M}\tau 1_M$
and equivariance give
$x_N=\sum_{\tau M\in N/M}\tau(x_M)
=\operatorname{Tr}_{S^M/S^N}(x_M)$.
Hence the family is trace coherent.
These constructions are inverse to each other.

It remains to characterize complete normality.
Let $H\leq G$ be open and let $N\in\mathcal U$
satisfy $N\subseteq H$.
The restriction of $\varphi^H$ to $N$-fixed points is
$(H/N,S^H) \to S^N$, where
$f \mapsto \sum_{hN\in H/N}f(hN)h(x_N)$.
Indeed, $\varphi^H$ sends the characteristic function
of $hN$ to $h(x_N)$.
This restriction is an isomorphism precisely when
$x_N$ is an $(H/N)$-normal basis generator for
$S^N/S^H$.

If every $x_N$ is completely normal, all these
finite-level restrictions are isomorphisms.
As $N$ ranges over the open normal subgroups of $G$
contained in $H$, their domains and codomains
exhaust $C(H,S^H)$ and $S$, respectively.
Thus $\varphi^H$ is an isomorphism.

Conversely, if every $\varphi^H$ is an isomorphism,
so is its restriction to $N$-fixed points.
Every subgroup of $G/N$ has the form $H/N$ for an
open subgroup $H$ containing $N$, and
$(S^N)^{H/N}=S^H$.
Consequently, each $x_N$ is completely normal.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:profiniteLenstra}
The same construction gives a natural bijection
between trace-coherent families of ordinary normal
basis generators at the finite Galois levels and
$G$-equivariant $R$-linear isomorphisms
$C(G,R)\to S$.
For Galois field extensions, these are the
isomorphisms appearing in Lenstra's infinite
normal basis theorem.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:profinite-galois}
Suppose that $K$ is infinite and
$|\mathcal U|\leq |K|$.
Let $\mathcal J\subseteq\mathcal U$ be directed
with $|\mathcal J|<|K|$.
Then every trace-coherent family
$(x_N)_{N\in\mathcal J}$ with
$x_N\in\mathcal{CN}_{G/N}(S^N/R)$, for $N\in\mathcal J$,
extends to a trace-coherent family of completely
normal basis generators indexed by all of
$\mathcal U$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For $N\in\mathcal U$, put $V_N=S^N$ and
$U_N=\mathcal{CN}_{G/N}(S^N/R)$.
Each $V_N$ is finite-dimensional over $K$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:completenormalbasis} shows that
$U_N$ is a nonempty Zariski-open subset of $V_N$.
For $M\subseteq N$, put
$p_{MN}=\operatorname{Tr}_{S^M/S^N}$.
These maps are $K$-linear and form an inverse
system by transitivity of trace.
Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:complete-normal-trace-lift}
to the $(G/M)$-Galois extension $S^M/R$ and the
normal subgroup $N/M$ gives $p_{MN}(U_M)=U_N$.
Moreover, $p_{MN}(V_M)$ is a Zariski-closed
linear subspace of $V_N$ containing the dense
subset $U_N$. Hence $p_{MN}(V_M)=V_N$.
All hypotheses of
Proposition~\ref{prop:relative-affine-open-limit}
are therefore satisfied, and its conclusion
gives the required extension.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
